entities.name: House of Bourbon in France
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The House of Bourbon in France, the senior French branch of the Bourbon dynasty ruling France from Henry IV's 1589 accession through Louis XVI's execution (1793) and then again in the Restoration period (1814-1830), encompasses the French royal line most directly associated with the absolute monarchy at Versailles, the French Revolution, and the ultimate end of Bourbon rule in France. Distinct from the Spanish Bourbons (still ruling) and Italian branches, the French Bourbons are history's most famous example of a dynasty felled by its own people's revolution.

The French Bourbon golden age — Louis XIV (r. 1643-1715, France's longest-reigning monarch at 72 years) built Versailles (constructed 1661-1710, employing 30,000 workers, symbol of absolute monarchy), waged the War of the Spanish Succession to install his grandson Philip V in Spain, and dominated European culture so thoroughly that French became the international language of diplomacy and aristocracy for the next 150 years. Louis XVI (r. 1774-1793) — well-meaning but indecisive — faced fiscal crisis (from Louis XIV's wars and Louis XV's court extravagance), convened the Estates-General (1789), and was overthrown when the Third Estate declared itself the National Assembly.

Louis XVI's execution by guillotine on January 21, 1793, followed by Marie Antoinette's October 1793, was the defining moment of the Revolution — transforming it from political reform to regicide. The Bourbon Restoration (Louis XVIII, 1814-1824; Charles X, 1824-1830) attempted to rebuild royal authority but ended when Charles X's reactionary ordinances triggered the July Revolution (1830) deposing him. The French Bourbons thus serve as history's foremost case study of a dynasty that failed to adapt to modernity.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The French Bourbon line — producing Louis XIV's absolute monarchy model, the French Revolution's regicide, and Versailles as Western civilization's defining palace — is among history's most studied dynasties: their failure to adapt to modernity caused the Revolution that remade Europe and inaugurated the modern democratic age.
